title: Mendel's peas
hook: an Augustinian friar in a monastery garden discovers the laws of heredity

segments.voice: Yesterday, a priest at a blackboard and a universe getting bigger. Your line was faith and science. Did you get a look at the firmament? Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

Behind the walls of an abbey in Brno, in what is now the Czech Republic, there's a narrow strip of garden. A friar in a dark habit is kneeling in it with a small brush. He is moving pollen from one pea flower to another by hand, then tying a little bag over the flower so no bee can undo his work. He writes everything down. Tall plants, short plants. Smooth peas, wrinkled peas. Yellow, green. Season after season, he plants, crosses, counts and records. His brothers sing the hours in the chapel, and he walks back out to the rows. His name is Gregor Mendel. Today, Mendel's peas.
screen: `A STRIP OF GARDEN BEHIND THE ABBEY.`

segments.voice: Mendel was an Augustinian friar, a member of a religious order that lives by a rule of prayer and shared life. His abbey valued learning, and sent him to study science. What he found in the garden was this: traits from the parent plants don't simply blend together like paint. Cross a tall pea with a short one, and the next generation can all come up tall. The shortness seems gone. But let those tall plants pollinate themselves, and in the next generation short ones come back. Something was being carried, hidden, and passed on, in units that kept their identity from one generation to the next. Today we call those units genes, and the study of them genetics. Mendel didn't have either word. He had peas, patience and a notebook. When he published his results, they drew little notice. He went on to become abbot, busy with the running of the house, and he died before the world caught up with what he'd seen. Later scientists, working on the same questions, found his paper and saw that he had already worked it out in a garden. The Bible's first chapter has an old line about exactly what he was watching. In the King James translation: "the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind." After his kind. Like gives rise to like. Genesis names the pattern; the friar counted how it works, row by row. Paul borrowed a gardener's picture too, writing about the church at Corinth: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." The planter and the waterer do their part, and then they wait. Mendel's whole method was that kind of waiting.

Here's the practice: tend something that grows. If there's a plant near you, go to it. Touch the soil. Is it dry? Water it, or turn it toward the light. If there's no plant, hold a seed, a bean, an apple pip, or simply picture one in your palm. Settle, and breathe. Think about everything packed into that small thing, waiting. You don't make it grow. You only give it what it needs and wait. If you pray, you can say Paul's line: I have planted, but God gave the increase. If you don't, simply stay with the patience of it for the full two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Mendel's peas. The garden experiments of Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, which showed that traits are passed on in units that can hide and return.
Your line: the monk's garden. Today, plant something, or water something already growing, and give it time without checking on it every hour. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Some religious orders, the Augustinians among them, keep gardens, schools and libraries alongside their life of prayer, and some of their members have worked as scientists.

notes: Claims rule: no dates (1856–1863, 1866, 1868, 1884, 1900) or plant counts given; the 3:1 ratio is described only as 'short ones come back'.
Mendel was an Augustinian friar at St Thomas's Abbey, Brno; the index calls him a friar and the carry 'the monk's garden'. Confirm both terms are acceptable together.
'His abbey sent him to study science' (University of Vienna); confirm phrasing.
'drew little notice' and rediscovery by later scientists (de Vries, Correns, Tschermak) stated without names or dates; confirm.
Hook details (brush, bags over flowers) describe his hand-pollination method in general terms; confirm.
Genesis 1:11 quoted as a fragment; 'like gives rise to like' is the script's gloss, not a scientific claim about the text.
